blocks.p: The meter is English heroic verse without rhyme, like that of Homer in Greek and of Virgil in Latin. Rhyme is no necessary part or true ornament of a poem or of good verse, especially in longer works; it was the invention of a barbarous age, meant to dress up wretched matter and lame meter. Some famous modern poets have since graced it, it is true, by their use of it, carried along by custom, but much to their own vexation, hindrance, and constraint, since it forced them to express many things otherwise, and for the most part worse, than they would have expressed them without it. Not without cause, then, some Italian and Spanish poets of the first rank have rejected rhyme in both longer and shorter works, as our best English tragedies did long ago, since rhyme in itself, to all judicious ears, is trivial and gives no true musical delight. That delight consists only in apt rhythm, the right number and weight of syllables, and the sense drawn out in varied ways from one line into the next, not in the jingling sound of like endings, a fault the learned ancients avoided both in poetry and in all good oratory. This neglect of rhyme, then, though it may perhaps seem a defect to common readers, is so far from being one that it should rather be valued as an example set, the first in English, of ancient liberty recovered for the heroic poem from the troublesome modern bondage of rhyming.
